planting.note: Set out rooted cuttings or grafted vines on a trellis in early spring once the soil is workable; this old Slovenian variety buds out relatively late, which helps it dodge spring frost even though it needs a long season to reach its characteristic high sugar levels.

directions: Žametovka is one of Slovenia's oldest named red wine grapes, long grown in Dolenjska (Lower Carniola) and Štajerska, and famous as the variety of the centuries-old 'Stara trta' vine still fruiting on a house wall in Maribor. It is a late-ripening variety needing roughly 170 days from budbreak to harvest in mid-October, producing large, loose clusters of 250-400 g that accumulate high sugar and give deep, pure red color with noticeable residual sweetness in simple wines. Train on a sturdy trellis in a warm, open site with good air movement, since the variety tolerates winter cold well but is more vulnerable to spring frosts during budbreak. Historically it was also used as a multi-purpose grape, both for light red wine and for fresh eating, and it remains a component of blended Dolenjska reds alongside other native Slovenian varieties.
sources: Univerza v Mariboru (Stara trta / Old Vine House)

planting.note: Plant grafted vines in early spring on a long-pruned trellis (šparon style) in an open, airy site; Zelen buds early and is demanding about moisture, so avoid waterlogged low spots and overly dry hillsides alike.

directions: Zelen is a white wine grape found only in Slovenia's Vipava Valley, where its name refers to the faint greenish cast of the finished wine. It is a moderately vigorous, early-budding, medium-early-ripening variety that struggles in shade and in soils that are either too wet or too dry, and it is quite susceptible to downy mildew, so a well-ventilated, sunny site with good drainage is essential. Its berries sit loosely in the cluster, which lets air move through and resist bunch rot, allowing growers to leave the fruit hanging longer to build flavor without excessive sugar. Use longer cane pruning methods traditional to the Vipava Valley and expect a dry to semi-dry wine of around 12% alcohol with crisp acidity rather than a big, ripe style.
sources: Vipava Valley Wine Route / Vipavska vinska cesta
Slovenian Ministry of Agriculture viticulture register

planting.note: Plant on elevated, sun-facing slopes with lean, marly soil rather than rich bottomland; Pinela performs poorly on fertile ground and needs the stress of poor soil to develop proper character.

directions: Pinela is an ancient white grape native to the Vipava Valley of western Slovenia, first documented in local records as far back as 1324 and today grown almost exclusively around Planina above Ajdovščina. It is adapted to poor, marl-based soils on elevated, sun-exposed sites, and modern plantings remain small, around 50 hectares as of the last official count, because the variety is particular about terroir and will not thrive on rich or shaded ground. Give it a warm, well-drained hillside and avoid over-fertilizing, since excess vigor and fertility dilute the delicate character that makes it valuable. It yields a light, crisp white wine and is often blended with other native Vipava varieties such as Zelen to round out acidity and aroma.
sources: Vipava Valley Wine Route / Vipavska vinska cesta
Slovenian Ministry of Agriculture viticulture register

planting.note: Set out grafted vines in spring on a trellis in a warm, open site; this late-ripening variety needs a full season to soften its naturally high acidity before harvest.

directions: Rumeni Plavec is an indigenous white grape of Slovenia's Bizeljsko-Sremič wine district in the far east of the country, known locally by synonyms such as debeli klešec. It ripens late and produces medium-to-large, elongated clusters of greenish-yellow berries that can blush reddish on the sun-exposed side, with thin skins and a fine waxy bloom. The resulting wine is light, tart, and modest in alcohol, which is why it is almost never bottled alone and instead gets blended into regional wines like Bizeljčan and the famous light red Cviček blend of Lower Carniola. Grow it on a trellis in full sun with free-draining soil, and rely on blending partners rather than expecting a stand-alone varietal bottling from the fruit.
sources: Slovenian Ministry of Agriculture viticulture register

planting.note: Broadcast or drill seed into a firm, weed-free seedbed in spring as soon as the ground is workable; this rhizomatous steppe grass establishes slowly from seed and needs a season or two to form a full sod.

directions: Known in its native range as sheep grass, Leymus chinensis is the dominant perennial forage grass of the Mongolian and Inner Mongolian steppe, spreading by rhizomes to form dense, drought- and cold-tolerant sod that underpins traditional nomadic grazing of sheep, goats, cattle, and horses. It tolerates saline-alkaline soils and extreme winter cold far better than most temperate pasture grasses, making it a mainstay cover and forage species on grasslands too harsh for conventional hay crops. Sow into a firm seedbed in full sun on well-drained ground, since seedlings establish slowly compared with the mature stand's vigorous rhizome spread, and avoid heavy early grazing while the sod is filling in. Once established it is managed by rotational grazing or hay cutting, and it is valued both for livestock nutrition and for stabilizing erodible steppe soils.
sources: Chinese Academy of Sciences grassland ecology research
